They will give it a shot and they will do it. But when they don’t want to do something, oh, that’s impossible.
Do you think that there’s some way to understand that some piece of media is generated by AI in a consistent and verifiable way? This to me seems like the challenge.

I am not as up on the literature here. Up to this point, there has been a pretty decent arms race. By definition, AI will continue to get better because — especially for visual models, for diffusion models — the way they work is that you have detection oracles that they test against. Certainly, you can never have something open source because it will immediately end up in the diffusion model. But for closed-source oracles where then you do not make it easy for them to test the oracle, one of the key things you do in trust and safety is then you have delayed enforcement mechanisms so they can’t brute force and test. I think it is quite possible.

Let’s say I was still at Meta. My advice to them would be to also explore a variety of different detection mechanisms outside of the content itself. I would do the best I can on the content, but I would also be doing as low level access as possible to the camera. I would only let content come from the camera.

And what I would say is, Nilay’s completely correct, there’s a massive hunger for, especially among young people, stuff that is authentic. I have three teenagers and they hate AI. They hate AI slop. They have a massive negative reaction. My wife and I created just a cute little family AI thing and they yell at us about a bunch of stuff, but they lost their minds about this cute little family AI thing because they just hate it.

So I think somebody is going to come and disrupt Instagram and it’s going to be because… There’s already, I’ve seen these little things where it’s like you take the photo during the day, be real and stuff. There’s these little things, but somebody’s going to massively disrupt Instagram because they’re taking the images of the photos straight off the camera and then all the editing is going to be only within the app and they’re going to do things to make sure that nothing can make it into the pipeline from AI. You’re going to allow some kind of CapCut-like functionality that never has an AI component. I think that is going to be a killer app.
Man, I could do another whole hour with you on this because the system you’re describing there is not detecting AI content, it is verifying real content.

It’s much easier. Verifying real content is much easier. And there’s been a big focus on this on the professional side, like Adobe has a whole thing where if you’re a New York Times photographer, you have a $5,000 Nikon or Canon camera, you take the photo and it’s cryptographically verified.
Yeah, but the iPhone that I’m holding here has that in it now. Right? Like there’s a lot of —
Right, the iPhone has it now.

Yeah. There’s a lot of this out there, but it’s the other side that I’m thinking about where it’s “We are going to detect AI text.” The leading model companies because of European regulations are now futzing with the text they generate.
Text is much harder because you just have so much less data. Especially in 140 characters, what do you have in there to detect? The more you’ve got, the more you can do.
It is amazing because I can detect Claude a mile away. So maybe I’ll just rely on my own human ability.
Yeah, but not in tweet length.
That’s true. The cheap ones, I can. But I’m just saying the notion that we’re going to verify what’s real instead of detecting what’s fake feels very important in the context of the media we consume.

Detecting what’s fake is always going to be probabilistic and we’re going to asymptotically approach impossibility, whereas detecting what’s real can be cryptographically perfect. I would not pick the battle that we will eventually lose. I would pick the battle that we can cryptographically win. That would be my suggestion.

And there’s somewhere in there where you have to build an entire chain of custody. We’re going to take the sensor data off the camera. We’re going to put it in a cloud server. We’re only going to allow edits on this server. That file will never get monkeyed with.

Sure, that’s true for the New York Times and Adobe Photoshop and stuff, but not for Instagram. For Instagram, you can do it all because it’s only the iPhone and it’s only Instagram. So the entire chain of custody is within your app, it is within the iPhone sensor and it’s in Instagram. So it’s actually easy for them.

Yeah. Look, like I said, We could do another whole hour on that because it feels like right next to the cybersecurity problem is the social engineering problem, and right next to the social engineering problem is the fake media problem.
No, absolutely.
How many phishing attacks are just “this website looked pretty real”?
Oh, yeah.

Or this person is talking to you or there’s an AI voice on the other side of the phone. And all of that comes down to whether you can detect what’s fake instead of verifying what’s real? And I don’t know the answer.

Oh, no. I’ve had to train my parents that, “If you get a video from your grandchildren saying they’ve been kidnapped, you have to call me because the odds that it’s real are not very high.” That’s where we’re at as a society.
I feel like I want to end on a hopeful note and I don’t know how to do it from there.
Wrong guest for that, buddy.

This is why you only come on every few years. Now after this, we’re going to do the series of birthday party guests. You’ve been talking about the dark ages. We’re in it, where it’s starting to accelerate. What are the markers people should look for in terms of progress to say, “Okay, we’re climbing our way back up”?

AI is great for lots of things. I think AI is going to enable individuals. We’re going to see a huge explosion of new companies. Stanford students have always been entrepreneurial, but the number of my students who are now starting two-, three-, four-person companies who are doing incredible things, who used to need to hire 50 or 100 people and take a ton of venture capital, is incredible. We’re going to continue to see that.

One of the things we hopefully see is a downtick in the number of major breaches at some point. We should hopefully see a downtick in the major CVEs that are wormable and that are in the fundamental infrastructure pieces kernel wheel. Like I said, I want Linux to be rewritten, but hopefully we see a downtick in the Linux kernel and those other kinds of libraries, openSSL, glibc, things like that.

Maybe I should vibe code this up, but I think it would be cool to have an index of where we are in the cycle, of like an artificial index of all of these, the Dow for all of the libraries of where we’re going. Plus right now, Patch Tuesday used to be like 150, 200, got to 300, 600. I think the last one was 900 something, so we’re geometrically growing. It’d be nice to see Patch Tuesday start to go back down. Apple patches are the same thing. Yep, you inspired me. I’m going to create a Dow index for this, the dark age index. And then maybe we can publish it on The Verge .
Yeah, that’d be great.

But I think these are the kinds of things that it would be nice to see a reversal for. What would be especially nice to see is that the day or actually like 30 days before you get the next version of OpenAI and Anthropic cyber models, that you don’t have this huge round of patches because what’s happening is those guys are running their models against Microsoft’s code, against a bunch of open source, and they’re giving all the bugs away and you don’t know where the bugs are coming from. It’s just like anonymous reports for 1,000 bugs in the Linux kernel. And then a month later, here’s the new Astra Cyber. So if those get smaller and smaller every time, then it means that we’re starting to reach some kind of steady state.
You should definitely do that tracker. We will definitely publish it. Alex, it has been incredible to have you on the show. We’ll have to talk again soon.
Yeah, thank you so much. I think you do some of the best journalism on this stuff and I really appreciate it.

articles.headline: Why you don't really need an expensive, high-end router
keyFacts: Budget routers under $100 handle most household internet needs because internet provider plans limit maximum home network speeds.
Essential features for most homes include gigabit Ethernet ports, parental controls, whole-home range, and Wi-Fi 6 standard support.
High-end routers are only worth buying for multi-gigabit fiber plans, wireless VR streaming, competitive gaming, or heavy home network file transfers.
body: Why you don't really need an expensive, high-end router
You may not be happy with the latest and greatest.

Speed has always been the main selling point for routers. Today's flagship models, like Netgear's Nighthawk RS700S, are rated for up to 19Gbps, come with two 10Gbps ports and eight antennas and sell for more than $500. For most households, that's money spent on a ceiling you'll never touch.

A budget router from a more affordable brand like Netgear or TP-Link, coming in at under $100, will handle the vast majority of what a typical home throws at it. Here's why you don't need a high-end router, and the few cases where spending more makes sense.
Start with the speed coming into your house

A router can't make your internet faster than your plan. The router takes the connection your provider delivers and shares it around your home, and that's the whole job. The FCC's benchmark for what is considered 'broadband' is 100Mbps down and 20Mbps up, so a budget broadband router only has to carry that to your devices without choking.

Before you shop, check what you're paying for. There is no sense in buying a router that transfers more data per second than what is coming in through your wall socket. A router rated far above your plan gives you nothing extra, because the bottleneck is the provider, not the box on your shelf.
What a good budget router actually needs
You don't need a novel-length spec sheet. Four things matter:
Gigabit Ethernet ports
Wired connections are still the most reliable way to hook up a desktop, a console or even a smart TV. Gigabit ports mean the router won't slow down anything plugged into it.
Parental controls
Useful for scheduling screen time and blocking sites on kids' devices. Most decent budget routers include them, often through a free app.
Wi-Fi 6 or better

It's not just about the speed. Wi-Fi 6 is a protocol that handles many devices at once more gracefully than older standards, and that's the real day-to-day improvement: Different devices around the house don't fight for bandwidth.
Whole-home range

Location is just as important as raw speed. A fast router in the wrong corner of the house might provide slow speeds where you actually sit. Match coverage to your space. In a larger home, a mesh kit or a second access point may help more than a pricier single router.
What Wi-Fi 7 adds, and who should get it

Wi-Fi 7 is the newest standard, and it's where most of the expensive routers live. Its headline feature is 320MHz channels in the 6GHz band, which the Wi-Fi Alliance says doubles throughput compared with Wi-Fi 6. This might sound like an enticing proposition, but there's a catch.

To see any of that speed, your devices need Wi-Fi 7 too, and plenty of phones and laptops in people's hands today don't have it. The top speeds quoted on the box are also theoretical maximums, not necessarily what you'll measure in your living room. Wi-Fi 7 routers do work with older devices, but those devices won't get faster just because the router did.
Match the router to your household

The right router depends on who's online. If you live alone or with a roommate, even an older Wi-Fi 5 router can usually handle your phones, laptops and TVs without trouble. In an average household of four to six people, with kids on their iPads, parents on their laptops and grandma gaming in the living room, Wi-Fi 6 is the safer choice because it's built to share the connection among many devices at once.

New, expensive, Wi-Fi 7-enabled routers only start to make sense in a big home or home office with a gigabit-plus fiber plan and plenty of Wi-Fi 7 devices to take advantage of it. If that isn't you, a budget router or a mesh system for a larger space will do the job for far less.
When a high-end router is worth it
In some cases, even a lone user can have a good reason to buy an expensive, high-end router:
Streaming PC VR wirelessly

Meta says Air Link over Wi-Fi works best on the 5GHz band, with the computer wired to the router by Ethernet, and it suggests considering a dedicated router if latency is a problem. A router with plenty of headroom keeps the headset's connection clean when everything else in the house is online.
Moving big files around your home network

Copying video projects to and from a NAS or running regular backups never touches your internet plan, so speeds depend on your own gear instead. Wired is still the best way to do this, but a faster router helps for any device that has to connect over Wi-Fi.
Gaming or live streaming
When a latency spike costs you a match or your viewers, a router with good traffic prioritization and spare capacity helps keep things steady.
A stacked smart home
Cameras, sensors, plugs and speakers add up, and a cheap router can struggle with the sheer number of connections.
If none of that is you, the extra cost buys headroom you won't use.
The short version: what to look for in a router
- Know your plan speed first, and don't pay for a router that outruns it.
- Pick Wi-Fi 6 or better, unless you live alone and have light needs.
- Get gigabit Ethernet ports and parental controls.
- Check that the range suits your space, and consider mesh for bigger homes.
- Don't pay for features your devices can't use yet.
- Spend more only if you stream wireless VR, move large files around your network or game and stream where latency matters.
Do that, and a router under $100 will likely do nearly everything you need.

articles.headline: Fireworks says you’re wasting money on AI unless you’re using all the models
keyFacts: Fireworks AI VP Rob Ferguson said companies waste money running AI models on-premise or relying on a single model.
Fireworks AI operates a platform that evaluates tasks and routes them to optimal AI models to maximize efficiency.
Ferguson claimed that routing tasks across multiple models can reduce a company's AI bill by at least 50 percent.
body: Fireworks AI is fine with helping companies run AI models in their own datacenters, though VP Rob Ferguson argues against doing so.

Ferguson told The Register in an interview that while Fireworks AI, a managed inference provider, supports on-prem AI, "we're trying to push people more and more away from it because frankly, it's just the economics."
The GPU hardware is just so expensive that if you can't keep it fully utilized, it's a waste of money, he contends. Ten thousand GPUs, he said, represent a billion dollars of capital.
"You don't want those things to be sitting idle," he said.

For companies with particularly sensitive workloads, Ferguson said, Fireworks is happy to work something out – it offers a service called Sovereign for just that purpose and it has partners like Microsoft that can help. But most inference work probably doesn't need that level of protection, he said.

"The state of the art for everyone is to have a portfolio of models," he explained. "In fact, I think most people don't know that the best model in the world's not Astra. The best model in the world's not Fable. The best model is literally a portfolio and we can prove it. You are always better routing between a few models than to do one singular model."

That's what Fireworks does through Nexus and its API, alongside competitors like Together AI, Baseten, and DeepInfra. As a managed inference platform, Fireworks AI routes inference tasks to whichever model, frontier model subscription, or API is best suited to handle them.
But the company is not just doing naive routing like an AI gateway. It's evaluating tasks as they come in and directing them to the optimal model.

"We build custom routers," Ferguson explained. "Our auto model is continuously updating so that we actually go through and we grade the difficulty of the task and we see if there're affinities that the models have, like Kimi is slightly better at JavaScript than Python, things like this."
The company's competitive edge, he contends, is its crack engineering team, which follows from its founders' work on PyTorch, a widely used open source machine learning library.

"We're performance experts both on the training and inference side," he explained. "People I think don't understand how important, for example, numerics is. So when you use a model, it's always called a mixture of experts – an expert is a different machine.

"And so you have all these different machines. It actually matters when you're training that you go back to precisely the right machine, because if you don't, the other machine will still answer the question, but it'll answer in a slightly different way. So we have to know how to build the topology to write back the data to the right space. We have to understand floating point precision [to handle very small values]. We have to be able to do all this where we're routing through a complex fabric through potentially more than one provider depending on what everything is. And so we're really systems experts."

Hyperscalers, he argues, will give you a GPU but then it's your responsibility to put it to use. Fireworks' advantage involves being able to maximize utilization at scale while maintaining model precision and speed.
Ferguson said AI keeps coming back to economics.

"People are just trying to figure out more and more things to use AI for and [to answer questions like] just how much more can I send to cached models, how much more can I send to open models, when do I need this specialization?" he said. "So we're constantly working with customers to help them come up with their own evaluation criteria."

One reason for this, Ferguson explained, is that frontier model companies are not transparent about their caching rates. He said Fireworks was working with a data science company and was caching about 90 percent of the tasks.

"We looked at [Anthropic's] Opus and it was caching 30 percent of the time," he said. "It was doing AI rework constantly. And with AI, rework is by far your biggest cost. If it's not hitting a cache, then your costs are absolutely insane. And so the token cost is not the real cost. It's the cost per task. And they're hiding that from you. And so we always tell our customers to be tracking cost per task, because that's the real number."
Another factor that companies should consider in their cost calculations, Ferguson suggested, is the value of their data and whether they're giving that data away for training.
"I think people grossly underestimate the value of their data," he said.

Fireworks AI has a zero data-retention policy, "but a lot of times," Ferguson said, "these other companies [do] not, and you should be getting paid for your data. Nobody really knew at the beginning of this current era that these models are memorizers. But now there's plenty of evidence that these models are. So if they're going to be using your data, then you should be getting value for it."
But it's not just about cost. Speed, said Ferguson, is underappreciated.

"Speed is the thing that people often don't know they can ask for," he said. "It's such a game changer for me and how I work with AI is so different when the responses come back as fast as I ask them."
What's the advantage of model ensembling, as the company refers to its model routing activities? A bill that's at least 50 percent smaller, Ferguson claims.

"So we say six to eight times cheaper," he said. "The reality is that because a lot of folks have a preference in their tooling, we kinda guarantee that in the case where you're still using a combo of closed and open models, we can always guarantee that your bill will drop by half right away. Like we're sure about that. And then the question is can we just get you to use more stuff?" ®

articles.headline: Linux on the desktop marches on as GOG announces its Galaxy client is getting a revamp headed to Windows, macOS, and your distro of choice
keyFacts: GOG announced that its GOG Galaxy launcher will receive a revamp in 2027 that expands support to Linux.
GOG stated the revamped Windows and Mac clients will run faster, while offline game installers remain available.
GOG also announced a community platform called GOG Social, with beta sign-ups currently available on its website.
body: GOG Galaxy—the DRM-free storefront's go at a desktop client and launcher—was always a nice dream that didn't measure up in reality. The pitch was: all your games, from all your PC game storefronts, in one centralised hub, but it never left beta in its 2.0 form and, in general, ran pretty poorly compared to its most obvious competition (Steam).

But that was old GOG. New, independent GOG has big plans for Galaxy. In the storefront's first "GOG Showcase", released Thursday, it announced the launcher would be getting a revamp in 2027, and it's coming to Linux too. "We know this has been a long time coming, but we wanted to do it properly: GOG Galaxy is officially heading to Linux", says the studio.

"At the same time, we’ve reworked the client on Windows and Mac to be simpler, run faster, and give you cleaner ways to view your library. Most importantly, our core promise stays untouched: GOG Galaxy is entirely optional. Your games are yours to download and keep through offline installers, exactly as they’ve always been".
That is to say, you'll still be able to find offline game installers in your GOG library if you want to prep for the digital ownership apocalypse (which, let me be clear, is probably a wise move).

Of course, if you're someone who plays games on Linux (cool people, I believe is the technical term), then you likely already have perhaps several tools which do the GOG Galaxy thing of letting you configure and install games from multiple storefronts: programs like Heroic, Faugus, or Lutris. Still, it'd be good to have a ship-shape Galaxy on multiple platforms, and a store with GOG's stature getting in on Linux is good news for PC gaming in general.

The Linuxification of everything isn't the only bit of news GOG released at its showcase. It also announced GOG Social: "a quiet, tidy hangout for actual game talk", meant to centralise discussion and socialising around "screenshot galleries, videos, and community polls with threaded replies and zero algorithmic noise".
If either of those things sounds cool to you, you can sign up for their respective betas over at GOG.
Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

One of Josh's first memories is of playing Quake 2 on the family computer when he was much too young to be doing that, and he's been irreparably game-brained ever since. His writing has been featured in Vice, Fanbyte, and the Financial Times. He'll play pretty much anything, and has written far too much on everything from visual novels to Assassin's Creed. His most profound loves are for CRPGs, immersive sims, and any game whose ambition outstrips its budget. He thinks you're all far too mean about Deus Ex: Invisible War.

articles.headline: Leeds United 1-0 Tottenham Hotspur: Premier League – live
keyFacts: Leeds United defeated Tottenham Hotspur 1-0 in a Premier League match through a 79th-minute goal from substitute Noah Okafor.
The victory moved Leeds United to eighth place in the Premier League table, leaving Tottenham Hotspur in tenth spot.
Tottenham manager Roberto De Zerbi stated he will miss the touchline for their next match against Ipswich after receiving a booking.
body: Roberto De Zerbi – who having picked up a booking today will be missing from the touchline for the visit of Ipswich in a fortnight’s time - talks to TNT. “The first half, we played well … the second half, we deserved to lose the game … we lost all duels … we didn’t play like we can … it’s a journey for us … we can learn from this game … there was a way to play better … to defend better … I am sorry for the result but most of all I am sorry for the performance in the second half … we didn’t play like a top team … we played without the right spirit, the right character, the right physicality in the duels … it is tough to accept this defeat after those good games in a row … but it is part of the journey … the most important thing is to understand why we didn’t play well in the second half … it’s just a mental aspect.”

As for the Bogle tackle: “Pedro Porro was [booked for] a normal duel … an incredible yellow card … the first situation of Mathys Tel I didn’t see so I can’t say … I have big confidence in the referee … nothing changes if he goes to watch the clip or not … there was the VAR … if they didn’t take the right decision, I don’t know … we have to keep our eyes on the performance, which can improve.”
He also reports that James Maddison was not fit enough to play much more than 15 minutes, hence his remaining on the bench.

Daniel Farke speaks to TNT Sports. “We are very happy against an in-form Tottenham side … the second half it was never in doubt … we missed a few chances but we were relentless … great commitment … great unity … fully deserved … Noah Okafor was a week out … so credit to the doctors … they told me to stay disciplined and only put him on the pitch for 15, 20 minutes … an ice-cold finish … we need to stay cool in the head … close the centre … be technically spot on … to be brave … committed in the moments when we can press … I think we found a good balance today … it’s good to have the winning feeling back in the dressing room, so credit to my boys.”

His view on the Bogle tackle: “I haven’t watched it back … there were several doubtful situations … a possible handball … I just know Jayden Bogle does nothing with any bad intention … it looked like a coming together … an unlucky outcome that Mathys [Tel] is injured … we wish him all the best … the last thing Bogle is, is a nasty player … he is probably the softest player in the whole league … I always call him my butterfly! … never he has bad intention, which I can guarantee, but of course I hope Mathys can recover quickly.”

Post-match postbag. “Thankfully, on NBC in the US, the Nevilles were on at halftime to explain that the Bogle tackle looks worse than it actually was, and that as fullbacks, they did that a thousand times in their career. Case closed!” – Robert Bodendorf

“The absurdity of the English ref clown show is making the Premier League unwatchable. They are far too concerned with narrative and managing the game rather than officiating it. You need no other evidence beyond them looking at a clear and obvious red card for five minutes with their hands over their heads as they agonise over giving Spurs a third match against ten men while Leeds need a win. It’s a joke and it’s going to kill off the ‘best league in the world’ status the Prem has right now” – Travis Antolik
“Not a penalty. The reverse angle shows it hits the shoulder, not a hand ball. Red card all day” – Conor Clarke

Noah Okafor speaks to TNT. “All I want is to help the team as much as I can … happy about the goal but more happy with the three points.” And here’s how those points change everything, ahead of what remains of matchday 10, with Spurs remaining in tenth spot and Leeds leapfrogging them into eighth.

Leeds celebrate their big win as local lads Kaiser Chiefs predict a riot. They were much the better side in the second half, the only surprise being the deciding goal took so long to arrive. Its scorer Noah Okafor wasn’t hanging around, mind: he’d only been on the pitch for 97 seconds when he found the net! On the balance of play, it’s a richly deserved victory for Leeds, who might have had a penalty early doors – conflicting pictorial evidence exists of the ball hitting Mateus Fernandes on the arm/shoulder, so pick your poison and take your position – then completely dominated the second half. The one huge elephant in the room, however, is Jayden Bogle’s crude connection with Mathys Tel’s achilles, which should have resulted in a first-half red card, and would surely have changed the course of the game. But here we are. Premier League football, at its wild and unpredictable best, for all its faults.

90 min +4: Williams-Barnett crosses from the left. Gray flicks on for Bentancur, free on the right-hand corner of the six-yard box! But Bentancur can’t control, and Trafford claims. Turns out Bentancur was clearly offside anyway. But Leeds hearts were in mouths for a hot second there.
90 min +3: Longstaff and Bogle – the latter very fortunate to still be around, at the risk of belabouring that particular point – are replaced by Rodon and Gruev.
90 min +2: Tonali dribbles down the left and finds Williams-Barnett in the box with a low cross. Williams-Barnett tries to sort his feet out for a shot, but can’t manage it. Leeds clear again.

90 min +1: Robertson swings a free kick in from the left. Van Hecke rises highest, and guides a header towards the top right. Trafford extends fully and tips around the post. The resulting corner leads to a throw, which is flung in illegally by Kulusevski. Pressure off!
88 min: Meanwhile, Leeds are doing a marvellous job of containing Spurs, who are trying to respond, but can’t get anywhere near their opponents’ box. Leeds’ xG is now exactly 2 to Tottenham’s 0.28.

84 min: Kudus makes way for the 18-year-old Williams-Barnett. When the game restarts, Calvert-Lewin once again tears clear down the right, but doesn’t back himself to shoot, turning around instead and laying off to Okafor. The move breaks down. That’s a couple of big chances butchered by Calvert-Lewin today.

82 min: Spurs haven’t won any of their last 49 matches in which they’ve gone behind. No wonder Roberto De Zerbi looks thoroughly miserable. That goal was no more than Leeds deserved; they’ve been by far the better team in this second half.
GOAL! Leeds United 1-0 Tottenham Hotspur (Okafor 79)

Bard throws in from the left. Wilson swivels just inside the box, chesting down and teeing up Okafor, who takes a touch infield before lashing a shot across Kinsky and into the bottom left! Lovely move, and what a substitution!
76 min: … but Spurs don’t clear their lines particularly well, and Tanaka strides down the left to win another Leeds corner. Longstaff, who must be wondering how he didn’t score, to take.

75 min: Bogle advances down the right and crosses low for Longstaff, who turns and launches a rising shot goalwards from 12 yards. It’s a superb effort, and heading in, but met by the fingertips of Kinsky. What a save! The ball clears the bar, and nothing comes of the corner.
73 min: Kulusevski and Bentancur combine down the right, but at such slow speed that Leeds close down all avenues to their box. Spurs have not created very much this afternoon.

70 min: Bard loops down the middle. Nmecha tries to loop over Kinsky, who tips onto the bar. But he was offside. Then Calvert-Lewin fails to hit the target. But Kinsky takes his sweet time over the restart, so the referee awards a corner to Leeds!

68 min: Spurs play some possession stuff. They don’t really go anywhere for a while, but suddenly spring into action, Gallagher bringing the ball down on the edge of the Leeds D before pearling a low drive inches wide of the bottom left. Not entirely sure Trafford was getting to that. Spurs fans thought that was in, so are jeered for their cheer not long after.

66 min: … so Spurs make a triple change, replacing the ineffective Marmoush and Fernandes, plus Porro, who is on one-and-a-half yellows, with Kulusevski, Bentancur and Gallagher. Gray will take over from Porro at right-back.

63 min: Calvert-Lewin, Bard and Longstaff combine well down the left. The ball’s rolled infield for Ampadu, who shoots from 25 yards. The ball takes a huge deflection to the left, and had it stayed on target, it was a goal, because Kinsky had committed to diving the other way. But it squeaks out for a corner, which Kinsky claims. Leeds are getting closer and closer.

62 min: Van de Ven again over-eggs his dribble out from the back. This time he loses the ball, allowing Nmecha to enter the box from the left and aim a curler towards the top right. It’s not a good effort, and easily blocked.

60 min: Porro clips Bard, who was advancing down the left, from behind. It should be a yellow. It’s not, though, presumably because it would have been a second yellow for Porro, and you know how referees process that sort of situation. Porro is now in the last-chance saloon. Meanwhile nothing comes of the resulting free kick.
56 min: Van de Ven over-elaborates when dribbling out from the back, and is nearly stripped by Longstaff. Had the Leeds man completed the challenge, he was through on goal. Van de Ven breathes out.

55 min: Tonali, dropping deep, tries to release Kudus down the right but has to settle for a corner. Kudus ambles across to take it. He exchanges passes with Solanke, then Robertson finally crosses long. Leeds deal with it. A bit of a waste.

53 min: Calvert-Lewin romps into space down the inside-right channel, chasing a fine Longstaff pass. He should shoot upon reaching the area, but lays off to Tanaka instead, who leans back and skies over the bar. Huge chance spurned.

52 min: Porro slides in, over the ball, and catches Nmecha on the shin. It’s a yellow. It should be a yellow. But Bogle’s far worse action in the first half should have been that at the very least. Roberto De Zerbi highlights this inherent contradiction, and is also booked for his trouble. Consistency? Good luck in your search for that.

50 min: Bogle crosses from the right. Calvert-Lewin prepares to sidefoot home from six yards, only for Van de Ven to nip in ahead of him, and slice the ball over his own bar and wide left. Then from the corner, hit long by Longstaff, Calvert-Lewin heads goalwards. Solanke blocks on his own line, then Elvedi heads wide left from close range. It should be 1-0.
46 min: Bard’s very first act is to whip in a glorious low cross from his position on the left. Calvert-Lewin is on his heels and can’t connect. That was begging to be rammed home.
Half-time postbag. “Both feet are off the ground. That’s Bogle’s entire weight on Tel’s Achilles. That can lead to a serious injury. Bizarre decision” – Martin Perring
“Why do red cards exist if not precisely to protect players?” – John from Norway

“The most insane thing about VAR, and there are so many insane things about it, is that we have to watch replays of a player OBVIOUSLY doing a red-card challenge one thousand times in slow-motion, and it ends with not even a yellow. The chicken-shit nature of it all, the incompetence, all elevated because of technology. I hate it so, so much” – Øivind Idsø

“There’s overthinking it, as you say, but this is like they’ve been given a task to find a reason for not giving that as a red, rocking and rolling desperately, frame-by-frame. The explanation they release for not giving a red should be a corker. Meanwhile, whatever happened to ‘clear and obvious’? VAR is almost single-handedly turning me into a grumpy old man. I’ll be off out now to shout at some pigeons” – Rob Knap

“I’ve supported VAR from the start. It was always going to have teething issues as it was implemented, and it was never going to 100% eliminate mistakes. Subjectivity is still a thing. But, my word, they don’t half make it hard to defend at times. It should be established now, a mature technology with most of the errors ironed out. If anything, though, It’s getting worse. I’m not in the ‘Bin it’ camp yet, but I’m a lot closer than I was at the start of the season” – Matt Dony
“Committees are an extremely useful method for decision making, especially when people have time to deliberate. But perhaps football refereeing isn’t suited to committees” – Kári Tulinius
“That would have been a red card at Elland Road in the 70s” – Gary Naylor

Leeds should have had a penalty; they should also have had a man sent off. The players walk down the tunnel. The referee was planning to drive away in his car, but the doors and square wheels have fallen off and there’s all smoke coming out of the radiator.
45 min +5: Ampadu throws long from the left. Van Hecke powers a header miles clear. Ampadu has another go. Van Hecke batters clear again. The xG does not change.
45 min +4: The xG, for what that’s worth, is 0.19 to 0.22. Meanwhile Roberto De Zerbi continues to give the fourth official the what-for. His post-match interview could make for good entertainment.
45 min +2: Fernandes slices a low drive miles off target. After nearly boiling over, this half is now fizzling out, which is probably for the best all round.
45 min: There will be six minutes of additional first-half time, most of which a result of the on-field referee and VAR spending ages failing to make a decision.
44 min: Kudus fizzes a tempting low cross through the Leeds six-yard box from the right. What a ball. But neither Gray nor Solanke respond. Any touch and it was the opening goal.

42 min: Marmoush clips Muharemovic from behind. That should be a booking as well, but the referee has lost control of this with his unwillingness to make any sort of decision whatsoever. Meanwhile Tel goes down, he looks really unhappy.

39 min: Roberto De Zerbi isn’t happy about that. You can’t blame him. Meanwhile the game restarts, with Bogle, who shouldn’t be on the pitch, crossing for Nmencha, who plants a header straight at Kinsky. Had that gone in, there would have been some wild scenes all right.
38 min: No red card, no serious foul play. That is preposterous enough in itself; that there’s not even a yellow is beyond a joke. The on-field referee should have seen that, at the very least.

34 min: Bogle leaves one on Tel, who was in the process of spinning him. It’s a really poor challenge, studs on ankle. A red card wouldn’t be out of the question here; there’s not even a yellow shown.

33 min: A long pass down the left confuses Elvedi into conceding a corner with a misjudged backwards header. One corner leads to another, then Marmoush heads harmlessly wide. To be fair, Trafford has had next to nothing to do as well, if you ignore a couple of long-range shots scuffed straight at him.

articles.headline: One Of Hollywood's Biggest Stars Just Auditioned For James Bond
keyFacts: Robert Pattinson, Nicholas Hoult, and others screen-tested for the role of James Bond, according to The Hollywood Reporter.
Pattinson recently worked with director Denis Villeneuve, who is making the next James Bond film, on Dune: Part 3.
Amazon has not commented on the testing, so observers must wait for an official Bond casting announcement.
body: As auditions for the next James Bond continue, new names are emerging and revealing which actors are up for the role. The latest on this from The Hollywood Reporter was particularly surprising, as it revealed some A-list Hollywood talent screen-tested for 007.
Robert Pattinson is up for the role of James Bond

The Hollywood Reporter revealed that Robert Pattinson tested alongside other actors for James Bond during the week of Oct. 24, but his name has only emerged now, around two weeks after it happened. Amazon, which now owns the rights to the franchise, has not commented on this and likely won't say anything until they officially cast a new James Bond.

While Twilight is what put Robert Pattinson on the map, he has since gone on to have a great career that spans critically acclaimed films like The Lighthouse and Primetime as well as crowd-pleasing blockbusters like The Batman and The Odyssey. He recently worked with director Denis Villeneuve, who's making the next Bond flick, on Dune: Part 3, and seemingly left a strong impression.

While the James Bond role historically hasn't gone to actors quite as famous as Pattinson is (it's often a star-making role itself), casting Pattinson would certainly draw eyes to Bond's return. Pattinson is far from the only actor currently up for James Bond, though. The Hollywood Reporter also revealed that Nicholas Hoult, who portrayed Lex Luthor in Superman, tested for the role alongside previously known names like Callum Turner, Jack Lowden, and Josh O'Connor.

One insider claims Turner has already been cast, but this new reporting suggests that may not be the case. For now, all we can do is wait for an official James Bond casting announcement, as studios tend not to comment on casting speculation like this. While the next James Bond film still does not have a theatrical release date, I'd expect that to change quickly once Villeneuve wraps up work on Dune: Part 3 and the starring role is cast.

articles.headline: Calley Means blames Susie Wiles and nepotism for stalling MAHA priorities
keyFacts: Former HHS adviser Calley Means claimed former White House chief of staff Susie Wiles stalled health priorities for sugar industry money.
Means also alleged that the White House prioritized special interests that hired Wiles's daughter at a lobbying firm.
President Trump announced that Wiles will move to his political operation, with Stephen Miller replacing her as chief of staff.
body: Calley Means, a former senior adviser for the Department of Health and Human Services , did not hold back when discussing his interactions with former White House chief of staff Susie Wiles in a Friday interview with podcaster Joe Rogan.

Means, who quit the Trump administration less than two weeks before the midterm elections , blamed Wiles for slowing progress on the Make America Healthy Again movement spearheaded by HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
Means was particularly upset by how Wiles, in his view, was motivated by money instead of making children’s diets healthier.

“Susie said to me many times: ‘We need money for the midterms, Calley. We need money for the midterms,'” Means said, noting she wanted money from the large-scale sugar industry. If the administration’s MAHA priorities were stalled, then the money would presumably keep coming.
One of Means’s policy proposals, which sought to require the food industry to address whether the sugar levels in children’s diets were appropriate, received opposition from the chief of staff.
“And that’s where Susie told me we can’t do that,” Means said, recounting what she allegedly told him. “‘I need the sugar industry money.'”

In the wide-ranging podcast episode , Means also said nepotism played a role in policy decisions at the White House. Wiles’s interests, according to Means, were particularly self-serving because they benefited her daughter, Katie Wiles, who works at a lobbying firm called Continental Strategy.

“Susie’s daughter went to a lobbying firm, and it was an open discussion in the White House. If a company hired Susie’s daughter, then that was getting a high priority,” he told Rogan. “So if you’re a special interest and you want to get something done, the secret’s out. You pay Susie’s daughter.”
Means primarily criticized Wiles rather than Kennedy or President Donald Trump , but he did emphasize his concern that special interest influences hold over the Trump administration.

Rogan’s two-hour interview with the MAHA activist arrived on the same day Trump announced Wiles was departing her role at the White House. She was replaced by White House deputy chief of staff for policy Stephen Miller . Trump thanked Wiles for her service, calling her one of his most trusted advisers.

“Susie Wiles, who has done an outstanding job, will be moving over to the Trump Political Operation,” he posted on Truth Social . “I want to thank her for her service as Chief of Staff — She has done a great job!”
Wiles, whose last day as chief of staff was Friday, said serving Trump had “been the honor of a lifetime” and that she was “so proud to have been a part of what we’ve accomplished together.”
MAHA ACTIVISTS CELEBRATE REPLACEMENT OF SUSIE WILES AS WHITE HOUSE CHIEF OF STAFF

Last month, Means resigned because he reportedly grew frustrated with disputes over food policy, among them the delay in creating a definition for ultra-processed foods and corresponding labeling requirements. During his tenure, he helped revise the national dietary guidelines and put animal-based proteins at the top of the new inverted food pyramid.

On the day of his resignation, Means credited Kennedy and Trump for laying out a “vision of combatting the entrenched, dark forces in DC that profit from Americans getting sick.” Over two weeks later, he was seemingly glad that Wiles was no longer Trump’s chief of staff.

articles.headline: ‘Horrendous feeling’ – James Trafford reveals how bad it got at Man City
keyFacts: James Trafford transferred from Manchester City to Leeds in a club-record £45 million deal this summer.
Trafford said he left Manchester City for his mental wellbeing after losing his starting spot to Gianluigi Donnarumma.
Trafford stated his goal is to become England's number one goalkeeper after recently starting for the national team.
body: James Trafford has revealed he left Manchester City for Leeds this summer for the sake of his mental wellbeing.
The England international sealed a dream return to the Etihad in the summer of 2025, two years after he first departed to join Burnley .
Trafford has kept four Premier League clean sheets in 10 games for Leeds this term Getty
However, disaster struck weeks later when the Citizens then signed Italy star Gianluigi Donnarumma in the same window.
This immediately saw Trafford relegated to second-choice, despite appearing set to become City’s No.1 when he first joined.
It meant that after starting the first three matches of the campaign, Trafford made just one further Premier League start in the following 35 games.
The 24-year-old then left the Etihad for Leeds in a club-record £45million move in the summer transfer window.
Since then, Trafford has been a standout performer in the top-flight and started for England over Jordan Pickford during the most recent international break.
Trafford: I lost myself at City
With Trafford flying high at Elland Road, the goalkeeper has now opened up on his struggles during his year back at Man City, and admitted a move away for first-team football was crucial.
On his time at City, Trafford told Football Daily’s The Football Interview: “What a horrendous, horrendous feeling. Not playing.
“You are ringing a lot of people and just venting. Like most people, you have a [bad] day at work and you ring someone up.
“I ring my dad, I ring my mum, I ring my missus, I ring my mates. I like ringing my mates and we can just have a good talk about it all. It’s quite funny.
He continued: “I had to play regularly this season for my own mental wellbeing. You just lose yourself not playing.
Despite a lack of Premier League minutes, Trafford was City’s first choice goalkeeper in domestic cup competitions last term and lifted two trophies Getty
Gianluigi Donnarumma’s European pedigree immediately saw him replace Trafford as Man City’s No.1 Getty
“Maybe I’m different, I don’t know, but the feeling of not playing every week, it felt horrendous.
“I just had to play every week this season for that mental feel-good and to keep progressing with my career and edging me closer to achieving the dreams I want to achieve.”
Despite his limited playing time, Trafford insisted there were valuable lessons from his final season at City, where he started in both of their Carabao Cup and FA Cup final victories at Wembley.
“Going into any season, I always have the highest of hopes and always the belief that it will go the best way it could,” he added.
“Unfortunately, we didn’t win all four trophies. It didn’t go how I expected it to go, but it happens.

“In the moment, I just tried to make the best of it as I could. Looking back, I don’t think it was a disappointing season in the end because I learned so much, I improved so much and I won two trophies in one year.
Trafford has earned four England caps to date Getty
“There were moments when I was very down, regretting things and feeling disappointed, but looking back, I’m very thankful for the experience. What an incredible year.”
In the same interview, Trafford shares his hopes at making the England No.1 shirt his own, having served as back-up to Jordan Pickford at the 2026 World Cup.
His strong form for Leeds was rewarded in the last international break, where he started in back-to-back Nations League games .
On his hopes of becoming England’s No.1, Trafford said: “It’s my aim and it’s something I’ve always dreamed of.
“I always believe that one day I could be. Every day I try to keep improving to put myself in the best position to be England’s number one one day.
“I think everyone in the goalkeeping department with the national team wants to be number one because it’s an amazing position to be in.”

articles.headline: Son of Iran's shah receives 'Freedom Prize' in Frankfurt
keyFacts: Iranian opposition leader Reza Pahlavi received the Freedom Prize from the Friedrich Naumann Foundation in Frankfurt.
Police reported about 18,000 supporters rallied for Pahlavi, while critics and several German political party branches protested the event.
Pahlavi said he holds the award temporarily until he can present it to a democratically elected government in Tehran.
body: Iranian opposition leader Reza Pahlavi on Saturday received a "Freedom Prize" in Frankfurt in the central German state of Hesse.
Some 18,000 people rallied to show support for Reza Pahlavi, according to a police statement.
The event was held at St Paul's Church. The building hosted the Germany's first-ever elected parliament in 1848-1849, known as the Frankfurt Assembly.
Pahlavi is the son of the last shah of Iran, Mohammed Reza Pahlavi, an autocrat who fled into exile after being deposed in a 1979 revolution.
The 1979 revolution was followed by the transformation of Iran into an Islamic republic and the consolidation of power around the Shiite Muslim clergy.
Pahlavi was handed the prize by the Friedrich Naumann Foundation, which is tied to the pro-business Free Democratic Party (FDP).
What did Reza Pahlavi say about the prize?
Pahlavi said that Iran "is a country not waiting to be taught democracy, this is a country being prevented from practicing it."
"A people ready to die for the right to vote is willing to exercise the right to vote," he said.
Rights groups say thousands were killed in a government crackdown on protests in January.
"You could not have chosen a people who better understand the meaning of the word 'freedom,'" he said.
He also stressed that he was receiving the prize only as a "trustee" until a democratically-elected government comes to power in Iran.
"I hold it only temporarily," he said. "One day I will place it in the hands of its rightful owners, not on foreign soil but in the capital, Tehran."
The speech was accompanied by chants of "Long live the shah, long live Iran!" from the crowd.

Pahlavi has in the past offered to lead a transitional government in the event of a democratic transition in the West Asian country and has said he does not aim to use this proposed position to reinstate the Iranian monarchy under his father's dynasty, instead planning to leave the decision to a later referendum.
Iranians criticize Freedom Prize for Pahlavi prince

While Pahlavi has emerged as a figurehead for factions within the anti-government protest movement, others have criticized him for his vocal support for Israel and have accused him of failing to distance himself from his father's autocratic rule.

Around 200 prisoners held in Iran signed a letter protesting Pahlavi's receipt of the prize, Sahar Sanaie, spokeswoman for the Society for German-Iranians in Hesse, was cited by the AFP news agency as saying.
The letter described him as the symbol of a "bygone dictatorship."

The Frankfurt branches of the center-left Social Democrats (SPD) and the environmentalist Greens boycotted the event and said he could not be considered a legitimate representative of the Iranian people.

Meanwhile, the socialist Left Party argued that the church could not by used as a venue for the event due to Frankfurt city statutes that prevent the use of places of worship for political gatherings.

articles.headline: Winners and losers of historic midterm elections that handed Dems control of Congress
keyFacts: Democrats won control of the Senate and achieved their largest House gains since 1974 in the midterm elections.
Representative Hakeem Jeffries is poised to become the first Black speaker of the House.
House Democrats plan to call administration officials and Trump allies to testify, according to incoming Oversight Chair Robert Garcia.
body: The midterm elections marked a historic shift in power, handing Democrats their biggest House gains since 1974 and control of the Senate.
But inside the wave were candidates whose campaign heroics, epic stumbles and late-breaking twists helped shape the outcome. Here are some of the winners and losers:
LOSERS
Darline Graham

She got appointed to the Senate after the sudden death of her brother Lindsey Graham, and was virtually handed the nomination by President Trump over more experienced Republicans. But Sen. Darline Graham (R-SC) torpedoed her own chances when she admitted on a debate stage that “I’m not that informed on national security,” losing to Democrat Dr. Annie Andrews in a heavily Republican state.
Your 401(K)

Markets have been spooked over the Dem takeover with socialists in their ranks, with regulations and attempted tax hikes to come. The $5,000-per-person check that Trump promised if Republicans won the House is also a goner.
Haley Stevens

Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) held Abdul El-Sayed to a thin margin in the primary before hugging him and endorsing him, then reversed course 72 hours before the election and backed Republican Rep. Mike Rogers — only to watch radical El-Sayed cruise to victory. Democrats say it spells the end of her career in the party.
Roger Marshall

He ignored his own campaign team by producing a ham-handed TV ad defending his medical practice’s pursuit of deadbeats in the courts — a blunder that made Sen. Roger Marshall the first Republican to lose a Senate race in Kansas since 1932.
Vivek Ramaswamy

The former GOP presidential candidate was already down in the polls in the Ohio governor race when he released a controversial ad featuring the estranged mother of opponent Amy Acton calling the Democrat a “liar.” Members of both parties condemned the billionaire for exploiting a victim of abuse (Acton wrote about leaving home at age 12 after being allegedly sexually abused by her stepfather).
Ken Paxton

Republicans suffered an historic loss in the Lone Star state after President Trump tipped the scales in the primary runoff, endorsing scandal-tarred state Attorney General Ken Paxton over incumbent US Sen. John Cornyn. Paxton got slammed by a 12-point double-digit defeat to Democratic state Rep. James Talarico.
North Carolina redistricting gurus

Where do you draw the line? Not in North Carolina, where Republican mapmakers pushed through new district lines in an effort to expand the state’s 10-4 party advantage. The redistricting move backfired and final results put Dems in line to score at least a 9-5 advantage thanks partly to the “dummymander” effort.
Elon Musk

Musk spent more than $200 million in his home state of Texas trying to stave off Talarico and other Democrats after mending fences with Trump. But Republicans lost every statewide race up and down the ballot and the state House.
President Trump
He barnstormed the country and told people to pretend he was on the ballot, after clearing the field for flawed candidates in battleground races. Now he faces a hostile Congress as a lame duck.
“Fake” Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.

The decoy campaign got exposed — and nearly blew up on Democratic nominee Mary Peltola, who was leading in a vote count that could stretch for days. It was reported that Peltola’s aides had recruited Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. — sharing a name with Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan — to siphon votes from the incumbent. Peltola denied knowing about the plot.
WINNERS
Ashley Moody

Republicans got wiped out up and down the East Coast and all three states directly north of Florida, but appointed Sen. Ashley Moody (R-Fla.) scored a narrow win over Democratic Socialist convert state Rep. Angie Nixon (D-Fla.), earning a full term with her 51-48 win.
Anthony Constantino

The Sticker Mule CEO slapped a huge Trump sign on top of his warehouse in upstate New York, then found himself in a surprisingly close race – but withstood the Democratic tsunami in a district Trump carried by 20 points in 2024.
Hakeem Jeffries

The Brooklyn-born Jeffries is poised to become the first black House speaker and the first from New York in more than a century. With a majority that’s the biggest since President Obama, he has room to maneuver if a new crop of socialists tries to impose its will on the caucus.
Chuck Schumer

Another New Yorker, Schumer, 75, stumbled in Maine over the Graham Platner fiasco and his pick lost the primary in Michigan. But he lined up some strong candidates and was running the table of tossup races even in states that haven’t voted Democratic in years.
AOC

She stumped for socialists and lefties across the country, pausing only for the occasional In-N-Out burger, building cred with activists in Michigan, California, and even upstate New York. Her broadening appeal, ability to fundraise nationally and increasing name recognition could fuel a 2028 White House run.
Defense lawyers

Some victorious Democrats were transparent about plans to start hauling administration officials or Trump allies in to testify in all manner of grievances, with incoming House Oversight Chair Robert Garcia issuing a two-word post on X: “Lawyer up.”
Start your day with all you need to know
Morning Report delivers the latest news, videos, photos and more.
Thanks for signing up!
Vladimir Lenin

Core communist concepts, such as the disciplined vanguard and systemic political injection, outlined by Lenin in his famous 1902 tome “What is to be done?” were replicated with stunning success by radical Dems. Now, moderate Democratic leaders may soon be asking the same question as they try to prevent their party and agenda from getting hijacked by socialists.
Ron DeSantis

Ron DeSantis wasn’t on the ballot. But the Florida governor’s state managed to survive a Democratic wave that took down Republicans in even more pro-Trump territory. That gives him a story to tell if his quest for the White House reawakens.
Elise Stefanik

Retiring Rep. Elise Stefanik (R-NY) dropped her run for governor but got the last laugh when Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman got trounced, saying the “low energy” candidate faced a “political reckoning.” She called for rebuilding the state party apparatus.
John Husted
He may have lost the Ohio Senate seat he was appointed to, but at least Sen. John Husted (R-Ohio) is no longer the butt of President Trump’s jokes.
